message.content:
**Answer**

The last common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) is a small, early mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago**.  
It belonged to the clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to many modern mammalian orders, including:

| Order | Modern representatives |
|-------|------------------------|
| Carnivora | Lions, tigers, bears, dogs, cats, etc. |
| Perissodactyla | Zebras, horses, rhinoceroses |
| Artiodactyla | Deer, cattle, pigs, giraffes, etc. |
| Chiroptera | Bats |
| Cetartiodactyla | Whales, dolphins, hippos, etc. |

So, while lions and zebras are very different today—one is a carnivorous big cat, the other an herbivorous odd‑toed ungulate—they share a common ancestor that was a small, likely insectivorous mammal from the late Cretaceous/early Paleogene period. This ancestor is the last common ancestor of the entire Laurasiatherian clade, not just the two species.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the entire clade that includes both. That would be the last common ancestor of the superorders Laurasiatheria? Actually Felidae is part of Laurasiatheria (Crown group). Equidae is also part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of the two would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes Carnivora, Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc. That ancestor would be a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. But maybe the question expects "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria." But the question might be simpler: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" The answer: "They share a common ancestor that is a mammal that lived about 70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is a small mammal that lived in the late Cretaceous." But maybe the user expects "the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals." But that seems too broad.

Alternatively, the question might be answered by referencing the "last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae" which is the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both families, which is the last common ancestor of the superorder Laurasiatheria. That ancestor would have lived around 70-80 million years ago.

Thus answer: "The last common ancestor of lion and zebra is a small mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria." Provide details: "It was likely a small, insectivorous mammal that gave rise to the lineages that eventually led to carnivores (including lions) and odd-toed ungulates (including zebras)." Also mention that the last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~100-120 million years ago). But the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria.

Thus answer accordingly.
